item.title: The Daily Star – Padma Barrage debate: Is Bangladesh repeating India's Farakka mistake?
item.description:
Professor Md Ataur Rahman's article in The Daily Star on 5 November, “Padma Barrage: Why Bangladesh needs it and the challenges ahead”, is the most careful case yet made for the project. It deserves a careful reply. I agree with much of it. A barrage, he writes, cannot create water. Sediment management must be part of how the structure is operated, not a maintenance chore for later. The 9,000-cusec downstream release should be reviewed rather than fixed. The feasibility and engineering reports should be made public. And the project should be run as an integrated river system rather than a standalone structure.

These are the right tests. My argument is that the Padma Barrage, as approved by ECNEC in May, fails them. Measured against Professor Rahman's own conditions, the design risks becoming what its critics fear: a second Farakka, built by Bangladesh on its own river.
The Farakka Barrage in India. Securing a reliable share of the Ganges' dry-season flow is a crucial precondition for the Padma Barrage project. File photo

The first condition already fails

Professor Rahman's first recommendation is to secure an adequate, reliable share of the dry-season Ganges flow. That is the precondition for everything else. Yet the 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires on 12 December, less than a month away, and no renewal is in sight.

The pressures run one way. Bihar blames Farakka for siltation and floods and opposes a renewal that maintains the status quo. West Bengal wants more water for its own needs. Under India's federal system, either state can stall New Delhi, as West Bengal did on the Teesta. New Delhi itself is moving away from fixed guarantees, such as the 1977-style clause Dhaka wants, towards shorter terms and availability-based formulae, with Indian demand met first.

Climate change is shrinking the lean-season flow before anyone sits down to share it. The water promised under a guarantee based on historical flows may simply not be there to deliver.

The monsoon is the mirror image. Farakka cannot hold back the Ganges during the monsoon. When Bihar's embankments are threatened, India opens the gates; New Delhi has directed that all 119 remain open. Bangladesh gets a trickle from January to May and a flood from July to September. Our own barrage cannot hold back that flood either. Its gates, too, must remain open from 10 July to 10 October. Its real storage window is when the river recedes from October to December, and after that it can only share out whatever India lets through.

Bangladesh must, therefore, plan for the absence of a guaranteed lean-season flow. A barrage designed on the assumption of one is designed on hope.
Sediment pathways in the Bengal Delta, showing the proposed Padma Barrage, the existing Farakka Barrage and sediment movement through the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna river system. Sediment is essential for sustaining floodplains and building coastal land. Map: Ahad Chowdhury.

The arithmetic of a second Farakka

The project is defended as a means of storing monsoon water for winter. The numbers do not support that description.

The pond holds about 2,900 million cubic metres. Released evenly from January to May, that volume would provide roughly 224 cubic metres per second, or about 7,900 cusecs. The 1996 treaty guaranteed Bangladesh 35,000 cusecs in alternating ten-day periods of the lean season. Storage alone cannot replace what Farakka withholds.

Professor Nazrul Islam and Professor Md Khalequzzaman have worked through the project's own figures in Prothom Alo. Maintaining a combined flow of 698 cubic metres per second in the five distributaries and at the Godagari and Bheramara pumping stations would require 209 cubic metres per second from storage, or only 30 per cent. The other 70 per cent would have to come from the Ganges' live dry-season flow of about 1,295 cubic metres per second. The flow at Pangsha would be split roughly 60:40, reducing the flow towards Goalando by about 40 per cent.

That is the meaning of a second Farakka. Farakka diverts the Ganges upstream to feed the Hooghly, leaving Bangladesh short of water. Pangsha would divert what remains into the southwest, leaving the lower Padma, the Arial Khan, the rivers of Barishal and the Meghna estuary short of water. The planned minimum release of about 9,000 cusecs in March and April is about one-eighth of the roughly 70,000 cusecs that flowed past Pangsha before Farakka.

Professor Rahman is right that the 9,000-cusec figure should not be fixed. But it should be determined by the needs of the river below the barrage, not by what is left after the southwest is served.
An aerial view of vast sandbars in the Padma River. The proposed Padma Barrage risks replicating Farakka's adverse downstream effects within Bangladesh itself. Photo: Rashed Shumon

Sediment: A geologist's objection

I welcome Professor Rahman's statement that sediment must be an operating component of the barrage. But the design does not yet show how that will happen.

The 18 under-sluices, set about 1.5 metres below the main gates, protect the structure and its intakes from bedload. They do not move fine sediment out of a long backwater, and they deliver nothing to the floodplains or the coast. Opening every gate from July to October lets the monsoon pulse pass. But storage begins when the gates close as the river recedes from October to December, when the Ganges still carries a heavy suspended load. That is when the pond will silt up. Professor Islam warns of siltation, erosion and flooding along a stretch of some 145 kilometres from Pangsha to Pankha. Bihar, upstream of Farakka, shows what a rising riverbed does to the people who live beside it.

We are told that Farakka already traps much of the Himalayan sediment load, so Pangsha will receive less. That argument cuts the other way. The sediment that escapes Farakka constitutes most of what the lower delta still receives. Trapping part of it again deepens the sediment starvation of a coast that must build land to keep pace with subsidence and rising seas.
A map showing the proposed Padma Barrage at Pangsha and associated river management works. Diverting water towards the southwest could deprive the lower Padma and its distributaries of adequate flows. Map: IWM

The question for the delta is not one of total tonnage. It is whether sediment still reaches the land that needs it: the floodplains, the tidal basins and the coast. I spent the mid-1980s at Louisiana State University and watched the Mississippi delta lose land because engineers controlled the river without heeding its geology. Padma Barrage risks becoming a Louisiana-style cautionary tale. Diverting more water into the Gorai also diverts sediment into a channel that has been silting up for decades. Without permanent works at the offtake, the revived rivers could choke within years.

The sedimentation projections to 2072 cited by Professor Rahman may answer these concerns. No one outside the project can know, because the projections have not been published.

Approved before questions were answered

Professor Rahman calls for the feasibility and engineering reports to be made public. So do the project's critics. The difference is that the critics asked before approval.

On 22 August, Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon (BAPA) held a discussion in Dhaka that put ten questions to the Bangladesh Water Development Board and its consultants. Where is the downstream impact assessment? How reliable are the predictions for sedimentation, flooding and erosion upstream? Could the barrage weaken our position in the Ganges talks? Why is planning based on outdated data? A month later, Professors Islam and Khalequzzaman reported that none of these questions had been answered and that the feasibility study and its annexes had not been released despite the Right to Information Act.

A Tk 34,497 crore project was approved first, only to be explained later. That is the sequence that gave us the Teesta Barrage, which, as Professor Islam has shown, turned a deep, meandering river into a wide, shallow, braided one. We cannot repeat it on the Ganges on a far grander scale.

There is a diplomatic cost as well. Bangladesh's strongest claim in the treaty talks is that it needs the Ganges' lean-season flow. Presenting the barrage as the answer to Farakka, one that requires no discussion with India, hands New Delhi an argument for releasing less water.
Hardinge Bridge in Pabna, a crucial monitoring point for Ganges flows entering Bangladesh. The proposed Padma Barrage must account for uncertain upstream water releases and declining dry-season flows. Photo: Anwar Ali

What Bangladesh should do instead

The southwest's crisis is real, and doing nothing is not an option. But the choice is not between this barrage and nothing.

1. Pause construction, not the debate. Publish the feasibility report, the sedimentation model and its inflow assumptions, and submit them to independent review before Phase I commits the project to the design.

2. Put the treaty first. Negotiate for a guarantee clause and an environmental flow, and become a party to the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention to strengthen Bangladesh's hand, as Professor Islam urges.

3. Model the worst case. Test the barrage against curtailed Indian releases and flows reduced by climate change, not the averages of the past.

4. Design for sediment, not storage. If a barrage is built, its operating rules must prioritise sediment continuity and riverbed levels over stored volume, with effective sediment bypassing.

5. Guarantee the river below Pangsha. Set a binding minimum flow for the lower Padma and the estuary based on their needs.

6. Build what works now. Remove the sluices and cross-dams that block the distributaries' offtakes, then dredge the offtakes. Restore beels and old river loops for off-channel storage. Extend tidal river management in the coastal polders. Move the southwest away from water-hungry Boro rice towards drought- and salt-tolerant crops.

Professor Rahman ends where I would: the project must be managed as an integrated system. A delta is such a system, comprising water and sediment together. The test for any intervention on the Ganges is the one Farakka failed: does sediment still reach the land that needs it? Until it can be demonstrated that the Padma Barrage will allow sediment to do so, it should not be built as designed.

Dr Ahad Chowdhury is a geologist and environmental scientist. He teaches in the Department of Geology, Geography, and Sustainability at Jefferson Community and Technical College in Louisville, Kentucky, USA.

item.title: The Daily Star – The price of being a good woman: Family, sacrifice and power in Bangladesh
item.description:
Bangladesh has spent decades celebrating women's advancement. Girls' education, women's employment in the garment industry, expanding professional opportunities and greater participation in public life have become important markers of national progress. Yet the 2024 Violence Against Women Survey, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) with technical support from UNFPA, presents a profoundly uncomfortable picture. Among ever-married women surveyed, 67.6 per cent reported experiencing controlling behaviour by an intimate partner during their lifetime. The same survey found that 75.9 per cent had experienced at least one form of intimate partner violence, using its broader measures of abuse.

These figures reveal a contradiction that Bangladesh's development narrative has not adequately confronted. Women have become increasingly visible as workers, earners and contributors to national prosperity. But greater economic participation has not necessarily brought a corresponding redistribution of authority within families. A woman may contribute substantially to household income while remaining subject to restrictions on her movements, relationships, reproductive decisions or use of her own earnings.

The contradiction is not simply that traditional attitudes have survived economic modernisation. More importantly, patriarchal arrangements can adapt to economic change. They may accommodate women's employment, benefit from their earnings and continue to demand their obedience. The question, therefore, is not whether Bangladeshi women have made progress. They undoubtedly have. It is why progress in women's economic participation can coexist with persistent inequalities in their intimate lives.

As the world marks the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, this tension deserves closer examination. Violence does not emerge independently of the social relationships in which people live. Nor can it be understood solely through its most visible manifestations. The distribution of authority within families, the moral expectations attached to womanhood and the material consequences of refusing to fulfil those expectations all shape women's vulnerability to coercion.

How patriarchy adapts to economic change

Bangladesh's transformation since independence has altered the relationship between women, work and family life. The expansion of export-oriented garment manufacturing from the 1980s created employment opportunities for large numbers of women. Improvements in girls' education, changes in fertility, urbanisation, microfinance initiatives and the growth of service-sector employment have also contributed to shifts in women's economic and social positions.

These developments have not followed a single trajectory. Employment has enabled some women to delay marriage, support their families, develop social networks and exercise greater influence over household decisions. Other women have encountered new forms of insecurity, including precarious employment, harassment and the expectation that paid work should not interfere with established domestic obligations.

The historical significance of women's employment lies partly in its challenge to the assumption that men are the household's principal economic providers. Yet challenging that assumption does not automatically dismantle the authority associated with it. A woman's earnings may become essential to maintaining the family's standard of living without granting her equal control over savings, property or major expenditure. Her employment may be celebrated as evidence of family success while decisions about her mobility, friendships or career remain subject to negotiation with husbands and relatives.
Shefali Begum, 35, earns Tk 300 a day ferrying passengers across a canal adjoining the Kirtankhola River in Barishal, carrying her 16-month-old daughter Sohana on her lap. The economy benefits from women's productive labour, while households continue to depend on their unpaid care work. The photograph was taken in Rasulpur, Barishal, on May 11, 2024. Photo: Titu Das

This is where a familiar understanding of empowerment becomes inadequate. Employment can improve bargaining power, but bargaining power depends on more than income. It is shaped by ownership of assets, access to independent resources, support from relatives, social expectations and the availability of alternatives if a relationship becomes intolerable.

Feminist economist Naila Kabeer's work on resources, agency and achievements is particularly useful here. Economic resources can expand the opportunities for women to make choices, but their possession does not establish whether meaningful choices are available or exercised. A woman may earn an income without controlling it. Conversely, another woman may exercise substantial household authority despite not participating in formal paid employment. The distinction matters because development indicators often measure participation more readily than power. A household can become wealthier without becoming more equal.

The moral economy of sacrifice

The unequal distribution of authority is sustained not only through material resources but also through ideas about what makes a woman respectable. The good daughter is expected to accommodate her family's wishes. The good wife preserves marital harmony. The good mother places her children's needs before her own. These expectations are neither unique to Bangladesh nor uniformly experienced by Bangladeshi women. Care, commitment and mutual responsibility are essential to family relationships, and many women find meaning and satisfaction in them. The difficulty arises when these virtues become obligations imposed disproportionately on women, while their capacity to refuse remains limited.

Consider the expectations surrounding paid employment. A woman who contributes financially may still be responsible for cooking, cleaning, childcare, caring for older relatives and managing the emotional demands of family life. Her ability to perform these responsibilities alongside professional work is frequently admired as a sign of exceptional resilience. But admiration can conceal an unequal arrangement. The question is why all this labour must be performed by the same person in the first place.

Feminist scholarship on social reproduction has demonstrated that economies depend on the everyday work of sustaining people and households. Children must be raised, workers fed, illnesses managed and relationships maintained. Much of this labour takes place outside formal markets, and women perform a disproportionate share of it.

In Bangladesh, the expansion of women's paid employment has made this contradiction particularly visible. The economy benefits from women's productive labour, while households continue to depend on their unpaid care work. Where men do not assume a comparable share of domestic responsibilities, women's economic advancement can increase their total workload rather than free up their time. The result is a peculiar model of progress: women are encouraged to become economically productive without necessarily being released from older expectations of self-sacrifice.

These arrangements are not inevitably abusive. Households distribute responsibilities in different ways, and inequalities may be negotiated without intimidation. But unequal obligations can become coercive when a woman's ability to disagree is constrained by threats, financial punishment, humiliation or fear. The distinction between obligation and coercion is essential. Families make demands on all their members. The problem begins when those demands become systematically unequal and one person's refusal carries consequences that others do not face. At that point, the language of family responsibility can become a means of exercising power.
Two women carry baskets of coal on their heads. Women's employment challenges the assumption that men are the household's principal economic providers, but does not automatically dismantle the authority associated with that role. Photo: Rashed Shumon

When authority becomes coercion

The 2024 BBS and UNFPA Violence Against Women Survey is important precisely because it examines forms of abuse that are often overlooked in public discussions. Alongside physical and sexual violence, the survey documents controlling behaviour and economic violence. Its findings indicate that controlling behaviour was the most frequently reported category among ever-married women. The categories overlap and reflect specific survey definitions; they should not be treated as interchangeable with legal findings of abuse. Nevertheless, the pattern raises important questions about how authority is exercised in intimate relationships.

Coercive control is useful as an analytical concept because it directs attention towards patterns of domination rather than isolated incidents. Monitoring someone's movements, restricting contact with relatives, controlling access to money or using intimidation to enforce obedience may, in combination, create conditions in which a person cannot exercise meaningful autonomy. The harm lies not only in individual restrictions but also in their cumulative effect.

A woman who anticipates punishment for disagreeing may begin adjusting her behaviour before any explicit threat is made. She may avoid visiting friends, abandon professional opportunities or surrender control over her earnings because previous attempts at independence have resulted in conflict or retaliation. Yet coercive control must not be confused with every disagreement or unequal arrangement within a marriage. Partners may disagree about spending, childcare or employment without either seeking to dominate the other. What distinguishes coercion is the systematic restriction of another person's freedom through intimidation, deprivation or punishment.

This distinction is particularly important in a society where the language of protection can sometimes legitimise restrictions. A husband may present surveillance as concern for his wife's safety. Relatives may justify restrictions on mobility by invoking family reputation. Financial control may be defended as responsible household management. The question is whether the woman concerned has a genuine opportunity to disagree. Where refusal is possible only at the cost of humiliation, deprivation or violence, the relationship between protection and control becomes difficult to ignore.

Why leaving is not simply a matter of choice

Public discussions of intimate partner violence frequently return to a deceptively simple question: why does a woman remain in an abusive relationship? The question assumes that leaving is primarily an individual decision. It overlooks the social and economic arrangements that determine whether departure is possible.

For a woman without independent housing, savings or secure employment, separation may threaten her immediate survival. For a mother, decisions about leaving may involve childcare, schooling, custody and the fear of losing contact with her children. Women who support ageing parents or other relatives may face additional financial obligations. Even women with substantial earnings can encounter constraints arising from property ownership, family pressure, reputational consequences or threats of retaliation. The capacity to leave is, therefore, unequally distributed.

Class shapes the options available, but not in a straightforward way. A low-income woman may lack the resources necessary to establish an independent household. A professional woman may have the financial means but face pressure to preserve a marriage because separation would threaten her family's social standing. Age, disability, location and kinship arrangements can create further differences. A woman who depends on a carer may face particular obstacles to reporting abuse. Someone living in a remote area may have limited access to legal assistance or safe accommodation.

These variations matter because the language of empowerment often assumes that women can exercise rights simply because those rights formally exist. The national survey also found that a substantial proportion of women experiencing violence had not disclosed their experiences to anyone. According to the BBS and UNFPA findings, approximately 62 per cent of survivors reported not having disclosed their experiences.

The figure does not establish a single explanation for silence. Women may fear retaliation, doubt that reporting will help, worry about their children or regard certain forms of behaviour as normal. Some may have previously sought assistance without receiving effective protection. What it does challenge is the assumption that silence indicates acceptance.

Disclosure itself can carry risks. A woman who reports abuse may be encouraged to reconcile, accused of damaging family honour or blamed for failing to preserve her marriage. The demand for compromise can become particularly troubling when it falls primarily on the person experiencing violence. The moral language surrounding family unity can, therefore, shape not only how abuse is experienced but also whether it can be challenged.
Bangladesh's achievements in women's employment and public participation are significant, but economic modernisation does not inevitably lead to gender equality. Photo: Star

The family is not outside politics

The household is often imagined as a private space governed by affection, obligation and personal relationships. But its organisation also reflects wider economic and political arrangements. Property laws and inheritance practices influence access to assets. Labour markets determine employment opportunities and income security. Public services affect how families distribute care. Housing costs, childcare provision and access to justice shape the consequences of separation.

These institutions do not determine every household relationship, but they establish the conditions within which individuals negotiate power. A woman who has secure housing, an independent income and access to effective legal assistance possesses alternatives that may be unavailable to someone without those resources. Such alternatives do not guarantee freedom from abuse, but they can alter the balance of power.

This is why the response to gender-based violence cannot be confined to criminal punishment. Legal accountability is essential, particularly where violence, intimidation or unlawful deprivation has occurred. But protection also depends on whether women can obtain assistance without becoming economically destitute or socially isolated. Shelters, legal aid, accessible healthcare, psychosocial support, childcare and effective referral systems are not peripheral welfare measures. They influence whether the right to leave an abusive relationship can be exercised in practice.

The same is true of women's access to property and control over their earnings. These issues reveal a limitation in approaches that treat empowerment primarily as an individual achievement. Women may be encouraged to become confident, financially literate and professionally successful while the institutional conditions restricting their choices remain largely unchanged. The emphasis then falls on women's capacity to overcome inequality rather than on the arrangements that reproduce it.

There is a similar problem with celebrating resilience. Resilience can describe extraordinary courage in difficult circumstances. But when it becomes the expected response to unequal responsibilities or abuse, it risks turning endurance into a feminine obligation. A woman should not have to demonstrate exceptional strength to exercise rights that others take for granted.
Age, disability, location and kinship arrangements shape women's access to resources and support. Women living in remote areas may face additional barriers to accessing legal assistance or safe accommodation. Photo:

Rethinking progress during the 16 Days

The 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence offers an opportunity to question not only violence itself but also the assumptions through which society interprets women's advancement. Bangladesh's achievements in girls' education, employment and public participation are real. They have expanded opportunities and altered relationships across generations. It would be historically inaccurate to dismiss these changes or portray Bangladeshi women as uniformly powerless.

Yet progress cannot be assessed solely through women's growing contribution to the economy. We must also examine whether they have greater control over resources, whether domestic responsibilities are shared more equitably, whether disagreement is respected and whether institutional support exists when intimate relationships become coercive.

These questions require attention to men as well as women. More equal family relationships cannot emerge through changes in women's behaviour alone. They also depend on men's participation in care, their willingness to relinquish unilateral authority and the social recognition that masculinity need not be organised around control.

They also require us to recognise the diversity of family life. Some households have developed genuinely reciprocal arrangements, while others continue to reproduce inequalities despite substantial economic change. Understanding this variation is more useful than treating Bangladeshi families as uniformly oppressive or imagining that economic modernisation inevitably produces equality.

The central contradiction remains. Bangladesh's economic transformation has changed what women contribute to their families. It has not always changed what their families believe they are entitled to demand in return.

A woman may now be expected to help finance the household while continuing to shoulder most of its care responsibilities. Her earnings may be welcomed without her independence being equally accepted. Her sacrifices may be praised even when the conditions demanding them remain unquestioned.

These contradictions do not make women's economic advancement meaningless. They demonstrate why economic participation, however important, cannot serve as a sufficient measure of freedom.

The more difficult measure lies in the everyday distribution of authority: who controls resources, who makes decisions, whose refusal is respected and who can leave without losing the means to live.

Until these questions become central to our understanding of progress, Bangladesh may continue to celebrate women's contributions while overlooking the unequal terms on which many are expected to make them.

Bangladesh has spent decades celebrating women's advancement. Girls' education, women's employment in the garment industry, expanding professional opportunities and greater participation in public life have become important markers of national progress. Yet the 2024 Violence Against Women Survey, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) with technical support from UNFPA, presents a profoundly uncomfortable picture. Among ever-married women surveyed, 67.6 per cent reported experiencing controlling behaviour by an intimate partner during their lifetime. The same survey found that 75.9 per cent had experienced at least one form of intimate partner violence, using its broader measures of abuse.

These figures reveal a contradiction that Bangladesh's development narrative has not adequately confronted. Women have become increasingly visible as workers, earners and contributors to national prosperity. But greater economic participation has not necessarily brought a corresponding redistribution of authority within families. A woman may contribute substantially to household income while remaining subject to restrictions on her movements, relationships, reproductive decisions or use of her own earnings.

The contradiction is not simply that traditional attitudes have survived economic modernisation. More importantly, patriarchal arrangements can adapt to economic change. They may accommodate women's employment, benefit from their earnings and continue to demand their obedience. The question, therefore, is not whether Bangladeshi women have made progress. They undoubtedly have. It is why progress in women's economic participation can coexist with persistent inequalities in their intimate lives.

As the world marks the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, this tension deserves closer examination. Violence does not emerge independently of the social relationships in which people live. Nor can it be understood solely through its most visible manifestations. The distribution of authority within families, the moral expectations attached to womanhood and the material consequences of refusing to fulfil those expectations all shape women's vulnerability to coercion.

How patriarchy adapts to economic change

Bangladesh's transformation since independence has altered the relationship between women, work and family life. The expansion of export-oriented garment manufacturing from the 1980s created employment opportunities for large numbers of women. Improvements in girls' education, changes in fertility, urbanisation, microfinance initiatives and the growth of service-sector employment have also contributed to shifts in women's economic and social positions.

These developments have not followed a single trajectory. Employment has enabled some women to delay marriage, support their families, develop social networks and exercise greater influence over household decisions. Other women have encountered new forms of insecurity, including precarious employment, harassment and the expectation that paid work should not interfere with established domestic obligations.

The historical significance of women's employment lies partly in its challenge to the assumption that men are the household's principal economic providers. Yet challenging that assumption does not automatically dismantle the authority associated with it. A woman's earnings may become essential to maintaining the family's standard of living without granting her equal control over savings, property or major expenditure. Her employment may be celebrated as evidence of family success while decisions about her mobility, friendships or career remain subject to negotiation with husbands and relatives.
Shefali Begum, 35, earns Tk 300 a day ferrying passengers across a canal adjoining the Kirtankhola River in Barishal, carrying her 16-month-old daughter Sohana on her lap. The economy benefits from women's productive labour, while households continue to depend on their unpaid care work. The photograph was taken in Rasulpur, Barishal, on May 11, 2024. Photo: Titu Das

This is where a familiar understanding of empowerment becomes inadequate. Employment can improve bargaining power, but bargaining power depends on more than income. It is shaped by ownership of assets, access to independent resources, support from relatives, social expectations and the availability of alternatives if a relationship becomes intolerable.

Feminist economist Naila Kabeer's work on resources, agency and achievements is particularly useful here. Economic resources can expand the opportunities for women to make choices, but their possession does not establish whether meaningful choices are available or exercised. A woman may earn an income without controlling it. Conversely, another woman may exercise substantial household authority despite not participating in formal paid employment. The distinction matters because development indicators often measure participation more readily than power. A household can become wealthier without becoming more equal.

The moral economy of sacrifice

The unequal distribution of authority is sustained not only through material resources but also through ideas about what makes a woman respectable. The good daughter is expected to accommodate her family's wishes. The good wife preserves marital harmony. The good mother places her children's needs before her own. These expectations are neither unique to Bangladesh nor uniformly experienced by Bangladeshi women. Care, commitment and mutual responsibility are essential to family relationships, and many women find meaning and satisfaction in them. The difficulty arises when these virtues become obligations imposed disproportionately on women, while their capacity to refuse remains limited.

Consider the expectations surrounding paid employment. A woman who contributes financially may still be responsible for cooking, cleaning, childcare, caring for older relatives and managing the emotional demands of family life. Her ability to perform these responsibilities alongside professional work is frequently admired as a sign of exceptional resilience. But admiration can conceal an unequal arrangement. The question is why all this labour must be performed by the same person in the first place.

Feminist scholarship on social reproduction has demonstrated that economies depend on the everyday work of sustaining people and households. Children must be raised, workers fed, illnesses managed and relationships maintained. Much of this labour takes place outside formal markets, and women perform a disproportionate share of it.

In Bangladesh, the expansion of women's paid employment has made this contradiction particularly visible. The economy benefits from women's productive labour, while households continue to depend on their unpaid care work. Where men do not assume a comparable share of domestic responsibilities, women's economic advancement can increase their total workload rather than free up their time. The result is a peculiar model of progress: women are encouraged to become economically productive without necessarily being released from older expectations of self-sacrifice.

These arrangements are not inevitably abusive. Households distribute responsibilities in different ways, and inequalities may be negotiated without intimidation. But unequal obligations can become coercive when a woman's ability to disagree is constrained by threats, financial punishment, humiliation or fear. The distinction between obligation and coercion is essential. Families make demands on all their members. The problem begins when those demands become systematically unequal and one person's refusal carries consequences that others do not face. At that point, the language of family responsibility can become a means of exercising power.
Two women carry baskets of coal on their heads. Women's employment challenges the assumption that men are the household's principal economic providers, but does not automatically dismantle the authority associated with that role. Photo: Rashed Shumon

When authority becomes coercion

The 2024 BBS and UNFPA Violence Against Women Survey is important precisely because it examines forms of abuse that are often overlooked in public discussions. Alongside physical and sexual violence, the survey documents controlling behaviour and economic violence. Its findings indicate that controlling behaviour was the most frequently reported category among ever-married women. The categories overlap and reflect specific survey definitions; they should not be treated as interchangeable with legal findings of abuse. Nevertheless, the pattern raises important questions about how authority is exercised in intimate relationships.

Coercive control is useful as an analytical concept because it directs attention towards patterns of domination rather than isolated incidents. Monitoring someone's movements, restricting contact with relatives, controlling access to money or using intimidation to enforce obedience may, in combination, create conditions in which a person cannot exercise meaningful autonomy. The harm lies not only in individual restrictions but also in their cumulative effect.

A woman who anticipates punishment for disagreeing may begin adjusting her behaviour before any explicit threat is made. She may avoid visiting friends, abandon professional opportunities or surrender control over her earnings because previous attempts at independence have resulted in conflict or retaliation. Yet coercive control must not be confused with every disagreement or unequal arrangement within a marriage. Partners may disagree about spending, childcare or employment without either seeking to dominate the other. What distinguishes coercion is the systematic restriction of another person's freedom through intimidation, deprivation or punishment.

This distinction is particularly important in a society where the language of protection can sometimes legitimise restrictions. A husband may present surveillance as concern for his wife's safety. Relatives may justify restrictions on mobility by invoking family reputation. Financial control may be defended as responsible household management. The question is whether the woman concerned has a genuine opportunity to disagree. Where refusal is possible only at the cost of humiliation, deprivation or violence, the relationship between protection and control becomes difficult to ignore.

Why leaving is not simply a matter of choice

Public discussions of intimate partner violence frequently return to a deceptively simple question: why does a woman remain in an abusive relationship? The question assumes that leaving is primarily an individual decision. It overlooks the social and economic arrangements that determine whether departure is possible.

For a woman without independent housing, savings or secure employment, separation may threaten her immediate survival. For a mother, decisions about leaving may involve childcare, schooling, custody and the fear of losing contact with her children. Women who support ageing parents or other relatives may face additional financial obligations. Even women with substantial earnings can encounter constraints arising from property ownership, family pressure, reputational consequences or threats of retaliation. The capacity to leave is, therefore, unequally distributed.

Class shapes the options available, but not in a straightforward way. A low-income woman may lack the resources necessary to establish an independent household. A professional woman may have the financial means but face pressure to preserve a marriage because separation would threaten her family's social standing. Age, disability, location and kinship arrangements can create further differences. A woman who depends on a carer may face particular obstacles to reporting abuse. Someone living in a remote area may have limited access to legal assistance or safe accommodation.

These variations matter because the language of empowerment often assumes that women can exercise rights simply because those rights formally exist. The national survey also found that a substantial proportion of women experiencing violence had not disclosed their experiences to anyone. According to the BBS and UNFPA findings, approximately 62 per cent of survivors reported not having disclosed their experiences.

The figure does not establish a single explanation for silence. Women may fear retaliation, doubt that reporting will help, worry about their children or regard certain forms of behaviour as normal. Some may have previously sought assistance without receiving effective protection. What it does challenge is the assumption that silence indicates acceptance.

Disclosure itself can carry risks. A woman who reports abuse may be encouraged to reconcile, accused of damaging family honour or blamed for failing to preserve her marriage. The demand for compromise can become particularly troubling when it falls primarily on the person experiencing violence. The moral language surrounding family unity can, therefore, shape not only how abuse is experienced but also whether it can be challenged.
Bangladesh's achievements in women's employment and public participation are significant, but economic modernisation does not inevitably lead to gender equality. Photo: Star

The family is not outside politics

The household is often imagined as a private space governed by affection, obligation and personal relationships. But its organisation also reflects wider economic and political arrangements. Property laws and inheritance practices influence access to assets. Labour markets determine employment opportunities and income security. Public services affect how families distribute care. Housing costs, childcare provision and access to justice shape the consequences of separation.

These institutions do not determine every household relationship, but they establish the conditions within which individuals negotiate power. A woman who has secure housing, an independent income and access to effective legal assistance possesses alternatives that may be unavailable to someone without those resources. Such alternatives do not guarantee freedom from abuse, but they can alter the balance of power.

This is why the response to gender-based violence cannot be confined to criminal punishment. Legal accountability is essential, particularly where violence, intimidation or unlawful deprivation has occurred. But protection also depends on whether women can obtain assistance without becoming economically destitute or socially isolated. Shelters, legal aid, accessible healthcare, psychosocial support, childcare and effective referral systems are not peripheral welfare measures. They influence whether the right to leave an abusive relationship can be exercised in practice.

The same is true of women's access to property and control over their earnings. These issues reveal a limitation in approaches that treat empowerment primarily as an individual achievement. Women may be encouraged to become confident, financially literate and professionally successful while the institutional conditions restricting their choices remain largely unchanged. The emphasis then falls on women's capacity to overcome inequality rather than on the arrangements that reproduce it.

There is a similar problem with celebrating resilience. Resilience can describe extraordinary courage in difficult circumstances. But when it becomes the expected response to unequal responsibilities or abuse, it risks turning endurance into a feminine obligation. A woman should not have to demonstrate exceptional strength to exercise rights that others take for granted.
Age, disability, location and kinship arrangements shape women's access to resources and support. Women living in remote areas may face additional barriers to accessing legal assistance or safe accommodation. Photo:

Rethinking progress during the 16 Days

The 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence offers an opportunity to question not only violence itself but also the assumptions through which society interprets women's advancement. Bangladesh's achievements in girls' education, employment and public participation are real. They have expanded opportunities and altered relationships across generations. It would be historically inaccurate to dismiss these changes or portray Bangladeshi women as uniformly powerless.

Yet progress cannot be assessed solely through women's growing contribution to the economy. We must also examine whether they have greater control over resources, whether domestic responsibilities are shared more equitably, whether disagreement is respected and whether institutional support exists when intimate relationships become coercive.

These questions require attention to men as well as women. More equal family relationships cannot emerge through changes in women's behaviour alone. They also depend on men's participation in care, their willingness to relinquish unilateral authority and the social recognition that masculinity need not be organised around control.

They also require us to recognise the diversity of family life. Some households have developed genuinely reciprocal arrangements, while others continue to reproduce inequalities despite substantial economic change. Understanding this variation is more useful than treating Bangladeshi families as uniformly oppressive or imagining that economic modernisation inevitably produces equality.

The central contradiction remains. Bangladesh's economic transformation has changed what women contribute to their families. It has not always changed what their families believe they are entitled to demand in return.

A woman may now be expected to help finance the household while continuing to shoulder most of its care responsibilities. Her earnings may be welcomed without her independence being equally accepted. Her sacrifices may be praised even when the conditions demanding them remain unquestioned.

These contradictions do not make women's economic advancement meaningless. They demonstrate why economic participation, however important, cannot serve as a sufficient measure of freedom.

The more difficult measure lies in the everyday distribution of authority: who controls resources, who makes decisions, whose refusal is respected and who can leave without losing the means to live.

Until these questions become central to our understanding of progress, Bangladesh may continue to celebrate women's contributions while overlooking the unequal terms on which many are expected to make them.

Lubna Ferdowsi is a multidisciplinary researcher and writer focusing on gender, identity, geopolitics, history, sociocultural issues and public policy.

item.title: The Daily Star – India, Pakistan and the changing priorities of US foreign policy
item.description:
A critical look at US-India relations is essential to understand US-Pakistan ties. It might help dispel a long-held public perception in Pakistan that US-India relations have somehow been a function of the ups and downs in US-Pakistan ties. And that in establishing the extraordinary relationship with India in the last couple of decades Washington has finally “chosen” India over Pakistan.

The foreign policy establishment acknowledges the cyclic nature of US-Pakistan relations. But uplifted by the recent fissures in US-India ties, charmed by President Trump’s compliments, infused by an enduring faith in the US-Pakistan alliance, and confident of Pakistan’s coveted geopolitical salience, it remains ever optimistic that Washington would come back, and relations would be rekindled to their “halcyon” days.

Both the public and official views need revision, based as they are on faulty assumptions that consider the two relationships as competitive and comparable. That is why one keeps hearing successive Pakistan leaders asking the US to treat the two countries equally, and arguing at home that Pakistan needs to keep a balance in relations with China and the US. This is an erroneous view.

The problem is Pakistan cannot wean itself away from the pride of having been a preferred ally of the US once upon a time. But this notion refers to a world of the Cold War days in which the US had a single interest in South Asia, which Pakistan was capable and India was unwilling to advance. That South Asia is no more.
US President Donald Trump meets Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir at the White House on September 25, 2025. Washington's renewed engagement with Islamabad need not come at India's expense. Photo: The White House

There is a new world out there. Its complexity and disorder present a multiplicity of security and strategic challenges, its globalised economy offers exceptional opportunities, and its uncertainty compels countries to hedge, expand, and diversify their partnerships. In this world, India and Pakistan would both have roles for the US, though relations with Pakistan would be transactional and of limited bandwidth, and with India strategic and broad-based. These are two different relations, and neither derives from the strength or weakness of the other, or is based on “choosing” one over the other.

Coming to US-India ties, beneath the trade dispute and H1-B visa frictions US-India strategic cooperation and economic relations continue to thrive. There is substantial collaboration on defence production, space, AI, and maritime security.

In a recent piece, Sameer Lalwani of the Carnegie Endowment pointed out that trade rose to its highest level of $240 billion last year. And the new 10-year framework for the US-India Major Defence Partnership calls for advanced exercises and closer defence-industrial ties. Major US tech companies pledged nearly $68bn towards AI infrastructure investments in India last year. Micron, a leading semiconductor firm, opened its first assembly and test facility in India early this year. And recently Applied Materials and Lam Research announced investments in India’s semiconductor industry.

Prime Minister Modi bruised President Trump’s ego by not acknowledging his role in the 2025 India-Pakistan ceasefire. But this has not impacted the substance of relations. Trump has not reversed ties; he has simply put a brake on them.
US President Donald Trump meets Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the White House on February 13, 2025. India remains strategically important to the US despite periodic diplomatic and economic tensions. Photo: The White House

As for tariffs, these have indeed caused strains but they are not India-specific; they are being applied across the board as Trump’s economic instrument and geopolitical weapon. The reality is he would not allow countries to become economic competitors and geopolitical rivals with America’s help and at its expense. US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in his speech at the Rai­sina Dialogue early this year that the US would not repeat mistakes made with China with India.

India was so pampered by President Biden and Trump in his first term that it came to have a sense of entitlement. Now it is complaining about losing its extra-special status.

Indians forget Washington’s critical help in many areas. The US, for instance, has long supported Indian indigenous technology development. GE engines have been central to India’s domestic fighter jet industry. India’s first indigenous fighter aircraft Tejas relied on an F-16 testbed, and its development of a fifth-generation fighter relies on US wind tunnels.

From Pakistan’s standpoint, what is im­­p­ortant is that US-India differences have not impinged on India’s importance for Wash­in­­gton in the US-China strategic competition. And it will likely endure. Any occasi­o­nal adjustment in it will not bring dividends for US-Pakistan ties. We need to delink the two relationships in our analysis.

The bottom line: the US will continue to engage both India and Pakistan as there are no alternatives to each relationship. The alternative to India is India, and the alternative to Pakistan remains Pakistan.

This article was first published under the title “The US & India” in Dawn, an ANN partner of The Daily Star on November 23rd, 2026.

Touqir Hussain is a former ambassador and adjunct professor at Georgetown University.

item.title: The Daily Star – Has the centre of global power shifted to Asia?
item.description:
It was a day to remember, 19 November 2026. G3 emerged as a new global leadership group; Shenzhen displayed to the world what an AI (artificial intelligence) future metropolitan would look like; the International Court of Justice (ICJ) confirmed Myanmar to be the first state to commit genocide; and the most brutal phase of the Ukraine war unleashed itself after Kirch Strait Bridge was bombed in Crimea two days earlier.  

If any country could tackle these, it was China. Never before had Asia managed world leadership in modern times. Indeed, never in the last four centuries has Europe been absent from such a parley. Was the changing global order being confirmed? 

Asia was not only at the steering-wheel, but host, President Xi Jinping, could choose the other front-row passenger. Would it be the damaged United States, as even its president, Donald J. Trump, sees it to be, or the pariah Russian president, Vladimir Putin?

Key issues discussed were also of a change-making nature.
Leaders pose for a group photograph at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, southern China, on 18 November 2026. The summit underscored Asia's growing geopolitical and economic influence. Photo: Reuters

APEC Masquerading China’s ascent

Beyond the G3, leaders of 21 countries of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathered for their 33rd meeting. Formed in 1989 by Australia and other Southeast Asian countries, Canada and the United States were the only outsiders in the 12-member club. New members in the neoliberal post-Cold War 1990s included Russia, four South American countries, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Vietnam. Europe’s APEC absence partly explains why it was not at Shenzhen, but arguably, since APEC emerged at a time of regional rivalries, the European Union’s single currency plans was one villain. Others included Schengen expansion from five members in 1985 to 29 today to build a tariff-free continent and EU membership expansion. These depicted a fortress-mindedness to outsiders. From that competition emerged Mercosur (1989) in South America, the North American Free Trade Agreement (1994), the Central American Free Trade Agreement (2004), and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) adopted Free Trade Agreement in 1992. Many have since fizzled amid globalizing trends, but one takeaway is how APEC’s Pacific and Indian Ocean tilts stole the show away from the Atlantic―the post-World War II backyard of Europe and the United States.

Shenzhen made China’s backyard the top-agenda item; and that backyard is global. Topping that agenda was the nuclear future. The world’s top-three nuclear powers had reasons to cling together against nuclear competition. On track to becoming the largest global economy, China wants no constraints to expanding its nuclear arsenal. It holds 600 or so warheads, the 3rd largest globally, but targeting 1,000 by 2030 (2nd-ranked Russia boasts about 1,800, and the top-ranked United States about 5,000; Britain has about 250, France nearly 300). 

Russia’s nuclear capabilities compensated for its poor military performances in Ukraine; and the United States will not relinquish its post-World War II nuclear leadership. With Germany, India, Israel, Japan, North Korea and Pakistan wanting to join France and Great Britain on the (secondary) nuclear list, G3 leaders rightfully sense nuclear anarchy. Trump’s split from Europe and bonding with Putin and Xi Jinping to control nuclear proliferation alarms U.S. allies. No nuclear agreement was made at Shenzhen, but preventing nuclear war and continuing negotiations became cardinal calls. This exercise is old, but shifting from Soviet-U.S. bilateral talks (SALT I, 1969-72; SALT II, 1972-79; and START, 1982-91) to trilateral negotiations is new.
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin at the Yalta Conference in February 1945. The Shenzhen summit has drawn comparisons with Yalta, which helped shape the postwar international order. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Preventing nuclear war invariably hugs U.N. principles and purposes, a warmer global leader initiative this time than recently. Although they were as disdainful of the U.N.’s International Criminal Court (which seeks Putin’s arrest), both Trump and Xi Jinping position the state above ICC. They remarkably proposed U.N. reforms, particularly to reduce business-thwarting vetoes. Some observers compared Shenzhen to the 1945 Yalta Conference. Though praised by both U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin in Yalta, their successors increasingly disrespect the world body. Is this a turning point? We do not know. Yet, since history suggests upcoming world leaders favoring global compasses and declining powers mixed responses, China is already building global institutions (Belt Road Initiative), but Russian and U.S. interests flip-flop between national and global platforms.

U.N. reform talks coincided with the groundbreaking ICJ’s genocide ruling. That Rohingya case exposes the tongue-twisting responses of these leaders.

Myanmar’s Genocide

Despite ICJ’s ruling, evicted Rohingyas will not be returning to Rakhine from foreign camps. This is evident from the failed China-mediated attempts to repatriate Rohingya refugees from the camps in Cox's Bazar. From pitting the military junta against political parties, Myanmar’s ongoing civil war now thrusts Rohingya militias (like the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army members) against evicted Rohingyas (as in Bangladesh). Buddhist Bamars hate Muslim Rohingyas genetically. Myanmar’s most democratic election, in 2015, portrayed this. Nobel prizewinner Aung San Suu Kyi won handsomely, but allowed the military crackdown upon Rohingyas in August 2017. She challenged Gambia’s genocide case before ICJ jurists in 2019.
Judge Yuji Iwasawa, president of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), presides over the delivery of the landmark judgment in the Rohingya genocide case brought against Myanmar by The Gambia in The Hague, the Netherlands, on 19 November 2026. The ruling exposes differences among major powers over international accountability. Photo: Reuters

China belittles the ICJ decision for not being “conducive” to peace and for “overreach[ing]” its jurisdiction. Russia’s response will not differ, nor too India’s. Sheltering the largest Rohingya influx, Bangladesh’s response might be tailored by China extending its ‘economic corridor’ from Myanmar (which uprooted Rohingyas in Rakhine), to Bangladesh. In sum, no stones may be immediately upturned by the ICJ decision.

Ukraine’s worsening fate

 This leaves the Ukrainian future unsettled, sparking wider war. Whereas the United States will shield behind its peace deals that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff launched this month in Abu Dhabi involving Russia for the first time, before Putin accepts any deal, he will avenge the Kirch Bridge bombing first, with full brutality. Europeans will not spare him. Their militarization is thickening, broadening war clouds. For a continent riddled by social protests over local issues, Europe stands at its own Rubicon. As democracy and multilateralism deteriorate amid populism and immigrant-bashing, war would sink an aging Europe.
A satellite image shows a collapsed section of the Kerch Strait Bridge linking Russia and Crimea following Ukrainian drone and missile strikes, on 19 November 2026. The attack raises the prospect of further escalation in the Ukraine war. Photo: Vantor/Handout via Reuters

Overview

Taiwan was not on the front-burner at Shenzhen. Its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States this February must pass Congress. That can only happen this year, as Congress is changing. This delay, however, helps Trump push his China card first, likely seeking rapprochement between China and Taiwan. Both Trump and Jinping have met thrice this year (nine times overall, five of them in his first term), Putin-Trump twice at Shenzhen (nine overall, six times in his first term) and Jinping-Putin four times this year (over 40 during Jinping’s tenure). Will such camaraderie defuse fissures? Change is more certain, bilaterally or trilaterally. 

China carries two weapons neither Russia nor the United States have: more economic resources at hand; and lower external battlefield costs. Russia and the United States, contrariwise, shift deeper into solvency. Xi Jinping could do at Shenzhen what his partners could not: cross his own Rubicon successfully, much in Julius Caesar’s style. Caesar eventually produced the Roman Empire; China lacks viable competitors to not do so. Jinping had the cards to take the summit in his desired direction, host and execute as ‘boss’ and leave no sour notes.

It was a day to remember, 19 November 2026. G3 emerged as a new global leadership group; Shenzhen displayed to the world what an AI (artificial intelligence) future metropolitan would look like; the International Court of Justice (ICJ) confirmed Myanmar to be the first state to commit genocide; and the most brutal phase of the Ukraine war unleashed itself after Kirch Strait Bridge was bombed in Crimea two days earlier.  

If any country could tackle these, it was China. Never before had Asia managed world leadership in modern times. Indeed, never in the last four centuries has Europe been absent from such a parley. Was the changing global order being confirmed? 

Asia was not only at the steering-wheel, but host, President Xi Jinping, could choose the other front-row passenger. Would it be the damaged United States, as even its president, Donald J. Trump, sees it to be, or the pariah Russian president, Vladimir Putin?

Key issues discussed were also of a change-making nature.
Leaders pose for a group photograph at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, southern China, on 18 November 2026. The summit underscored Asia's growing geopolitical and economic influence. Photo: Reuters

APEC Masquerading China’s ascent

Beyond the G3, leaders of 21 countries of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathered for their 33rd meeting. Formed in 1989 by Australia and other Southeast Asian countries, Canada and the United States were the only outsiders in the 12-member club. New members in the neoliberal post-Cold War 1990s included Russia, four South American countries, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Vietnam. Europe’s APEC absence partly explains why it was not at Shenzhen, but arguably, since APEC emerged at a time of regional rivalries, the European Union’s single currency plans was one villain. Others included Schengen expansion from five members in 1985 to 29 today to build a tariff-free continent and EU membership expansion. These depicted a fortress-mindedness to outsiders. From that competition emerged Mercosur (1989) in South America, the North American Free Trade Agreement (1994), the Central American Free Trade Agreement (2004), and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) adopted Free Trade Agreement in 1992. Many have since fizzled amid globalizing trends, but one takeaway is how APEC’s Pacific and Indian Ocean tilts stole the show away from the Atlantic―the post-World War II backyard of Europe and the United States.

Shenzhen made China’s backyard the top-agenda item; and that backyard is global. Topping that agenda was the nuclear future. The world’s top-three nuclear powers had reasons to cling together against nuclear competition. On track to becoming the largest global economy, China wants no constraints to expanding its nuclear arsenal. It holds 600 or so warheads, the 3rd largest globally, but targeting 1,000 by 2030 (2nd-ranked Russia boasts about 1,800, and the top-ranked United States about 5,000; Britain has about 250, France nearly 300). 

Russia’s nuclear capabilities compensated for its poor military performances in Ukraine; and the United States will not relinquish its post-World War II nuclear leadership. With Germany, India, Israel, Japan, North Korea and Pakistan wanting to join France and Great Britain on the (secondary) nuclear list, G3 leaders rightfully sense nuclear anarchy. Trump’s split from Europe and bonding with Putin and Xi Jinping to control nuclear proliferation alarms U.S. allies. No nuclear agreement was made at Shenzhen, but preventing nuclear war and continuing negotiations became cardinal calls. This exercise is old, but shifting from Soviet-U.S. bilateral talks (SALT I, 1969-72; SALT II, 1972-79; and START, 1982-91) to trilateral negotiations is new.
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin at the Yalta Conference in February 1945. The Shenzhen summit has drawn comparisons with Yalta, which helped shape the postwar international order. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Preventing nuclear war invariably hugs U.N. principles and purposes, a warmer global leader initiative this time than recently. Although they were as disdainful of the U.N.’s International Criminal Court (which seeks Putin’s arrest), both Trump and Xi Jinping position the state above ICC. They remarkably proposed U.N. reforms, particularly to reduce business-thwarting vetoes. Some observers compared Shenzhen to the 1945 Yalta Conference. Though praised by both U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin in Yalta, their successors increasingly disrespect the world body. Is this a turning point? We do not know. Yet, since history suggests upcoming world leaders favoring global compasses and declining powers mixed responses, China is already building global institutions (Belt Road Initiative), but Russian and U.S. interests flip-flop between national and global platforms.

U.N. reform talks coincided with the groundbreaking ICJ’s genocide ruling. That Rohingya case exposes the tongue-twisting responses of these leaders.

Myanmar’s Genocide

Despite ICJ’s ruling, evicted Rohingyas will not be returning to Rakhine from foreign camps. This is evident from the failed China-mediated attempts to repatriate Rohingya refugees from the camps in Cox's Bazar. From pitting the military junta against political parties, Myanmar’s ongoing civil war now thrusts Rohingya militias (like the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army members) against evicted Rohingyas (as in Bangladesh). Buddhist Bamars hate Muslim Rohingyas genetically. Myanmar’s most democratic election, in 2015, portrayed this. Nobel prizewinner Aung San Suu Kyi won handsomely, but allowed the military crackdown upon Rohingyas in August 2017. She challenged Gambia’s genocide case before ICJ jurists in 2019.
Judge Yuji Iwasawa, president of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), presides over the delivery of the landmark judgment in the Rohingya genocide case brought against Myanmar by The Gambia in The Hague, the Netherlands, on 19 November 2026. The ruling exposes differences among major powers over international accountability. Photo: Reuters

China belittles the ICJ decision for not being “conducive” to peace and for “overreach[ing]” its jurisdiction. Russia’s response will not differ, nor too India’s. Sheltering the largest Rohingya influx, Bangladesh’s response might be tailored by China extending its ‘economic corridor’ from Myanmar (which uprooted Rohingyas in Rakhine), to Bangladesh. In sum, no stones may be immediately upturned by the ICJ decision.

 This leaves the Ukrainian future unsettled, sparking wider war. Whereas the United States will shield behind its peace deals that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff launched this month in Abu Dhabi involving Russia for the first time, before Putin accepts any deal, he will avenge the Kirch Bridge bombing first, with full brutality.
