item.title: The Daily Star – Before Plassey: The origins of the East India Company’s land grab in Bengal
item.description:
In late 1698, Charles Eyre, soon to be appointed governor of Fort William in Bengal, persuaded the viceroy, Prince Azim ush Shan, to grant the East India Company a nishan conferring zamindari rights over the three small townships of Sutanuti, Kalkata and Govindpur in exchange for Rs 16,000 and a liberal disbursement of bribes. It was a move later described by Walter Firminger as the most significant and enduring step taken by the Company between 1690 and 1757 (Walter Firminger, Historical Introduction to the Bengal Portion of ‘The Fifth Report’, Cambray, Calcutta, 1917, p. 374). Firminger has to be taken seriously, and so I wish to investigate briefly how the events of 1698 can be situated within the Company’s quest to acquire territory, in the course of which it transformed from a venture concerned principally, but not exclusively, with commerce and trade into a colonising power that came to rule over large parts of the Indian subcontinent (see my Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, on which I have drawn here).

The acquisition of land in India has attracted scholarly interest, but for understandable reasons, the events of the eighteenth century have tended to provide the focus. This was a period, after all, when, following Clive’s victory at Palashi in 1757, the Company acquired territory in Bengal and Bihar on a scale that dwarfed its earlier territorial gains. Compared with the enormity of this land grab, the acquisitions of the seventeenth century were minute, and yet I suspected that in the early decades of the Company, the legal, economic and political foundations were laid for the wholesale plunder that was to follow (see Philip Stern, The Company State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundation of the British Empire in India, Oxford University Press, 2011; and David Veevers, The Origins of the British Empire in Asia, 1600–1750, Cambridge University Press, 2019). 
 
A modern reconstruction shows Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindpur, the three settlements over which the East India Company acquired zamindari rights in 1698. Map: P. K. Niyogi/Wikimedia Commons.

Indeed, the signs were there from the very start. Hidden amidst the technicalities of the Company's 1600 charter was a clause that empowered it to acquire, retain and dispose of land, not a provision, it has to be said, that we would expect to find in the founding charter of a private, joint-stock company putatively engaged in commerce. The limited power of these seemingly hubristic sentiments, however, was soon exposed by the conditions early factors encountered in India. Not only were they treated with disdain by Mughal authorities, but the futility of the notion that land could be annexed in the face of opposition from an empire with a massive land army soon came to be recognised. Somewhat against the odds, however, the Company was able to lease a commodious house at the great port of Surat, but the factors were only too aware of their vulnerabilities. They could not resist threats to vacate the premises at a moment’s notice, and Mughal officials repeatedly denied them permission to convert the factory into a defensible space by fortifying it.

Frustrated by the intransigence of Mughal authorities and repeated failures to consolidate its position at Surat, the Company turned its attention to the Coromandel Coast on the eastern side of India. Over the ensuing decades, partly through circumstance and partly through political manoeuvring, relatively secure bases were established, most notably in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, which emerged as the three principal sites of the Raj. Our understanding of this process is, however, fragile. What is clear is that early incursions were secured through negotiations between Company agents and indigenous authorities, the details of which cannot be fully grasped without an intimate knowledge of competing systems of land administration and the laws governing land, as well as an appreciation of regional balances of political power.
The cover of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India by John Marriott, published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

Key to this was the relatively small coterie of Company agents who, by forming a branch of subimperialism, effectively conducted affairs in India (see Eric Stokes, The Peasant and the Raj: Studies in Agrarian Society and Peasant Rebellion in Colonial India, Cambridge University Press, 1973). Given that it took six months for a communication from the directors in London to reach India, the agents, legitimately claiming that they knew conditions on the ground best, were able to act autonomously in all spheres of Company endeavour, including the acquisition of land. Under these circumstances, we might have expected some among them to be versed in land law as a precondition for entering into negotiations with indigenous authorities. This, however, was never the case. To the best of my knowledge, no factor was trained in, or indeed possessed even a rudimentary knowledge of, English land law, let alone Mughal or Hindu codes governing the administration of land. The directors were aware of this deficiency and attempted to address it by shipping out small collections of standard legal texts, but it was a futile gesture.

Two urgent questions arise: How did Company agents approach negotiations over land, and to what extent were these conducted within a framework set by English common law? It seems to me that pragmatism, rather than a coherent, unified strategy, held the key to eventual success. In a piece mischievously entitled ‘In Defense of Ignorance’, Lauren Benton surveys recent work on the legal politics of the Atlantic world in the early modern period (Lauren Benton, ‘In Defense of Ignorance: Frameworks for Legal Politics in the Atlantic World’, in Brian Owensby and Richard Ross (eds), Negotiating Legal Intelligibility in British, Iberian and Indigenous America, New York University Press, 2018). In legal negotiations with Native American communities, she argues, there was a clear separation on both sides between intelligibility and understanding. The absence of legal training among colonisers did not compromise their position; indigenous legal codes became intelligible to them as agents came to know them through experience and the application of more familiar legal analogies. Put simply, they developed the skills to read the legal landscape and act strategically, often in a shifting political climate, to reach settlements that furthered their interests. ‘Understanding is overrated,’ Benton concludes, ‘both as a legal capacity and as an object of historical inquiry. Abilities to “read” political-legal constraints and to engage in legal practices with even basic competence, in contrast, brought enormous dividends.’
 
An imagined meeting between Robert Clive and Mir Jafar after the Battle of Palashi in 1757. The Company’s later territorial gains dwarfed the small acquisitions of the preceding century. Painting: Francis Hayman, c. 1760; National Portrait Gallery/Wikimedia Commons.

I see agents acting with the same intelligibility as the Company strove to acquire territory in the seventeenth century. When its interests turned to the Coromandel Coast, the site chosen was an unprepossessing fishing village with few natural advantages. The directors initially disapproved of any notion of establishing a settlement, but the agents recognised the potential of Madras, which, crucially, being located in a region beyond Mughal control, would not be subject to the same intransigence experienced in Surat. Indeed, in what was a febrile political climate punctuated by warring factions, the local nayak, Venkatappa, saw in an alliance with the Company an opportunity to boost trade and strengthen his position against rival kingdoms. The kaul subsequently granted in 1638 contained unprecedented concessions, including the right to build a fort and the authority to govern Madras for two years. Because the nayak did not hold alienable rights over the land, however, the Company viewed the arrangement through the lens of common law as a fief under his suzerainty.

This plot, largely infertile and providing, at best, poor foundations for buildings, measured only four square miles, but it was to become the Company's first permanent settlement in India. The initial kaul was renewed, and little time was lost in building what became Fort St George. The security it offered attracted native artisans seeking refuge from the conflicts. They settled outside the walls in their thousands, and the population soared. By 1680, the population of Madras stood at approximately 300,000. In a remarkable missive to the St George council, Josiah Child, the most rapacious of Company chairmen, declared that the place might well provide the foundation of a permanent English dominion in India.
Fort St George at Madras, depicted in an eighteenth-century print. Founded on the Coromandel Coast in the 1630s, the settlement gave the Company a fortified base beyond Mughal control. Source: detail of a print published by J. Fielding in 1782, in John Marriott’s collection.

The next great centre of empire, Bombay, was acquired and grew under very different circumstances. Since 1534, when Sultan Bahadur signed a treaty conferring rights on the Portuguese, the small island and port had languished through neglect and were generally considered to have few prospects. The beleaguered Company at Surat, however, looked to Bombay as a means of opening up trade along the west coast, but the Portuguese resisted any such move. Then, in one of those remarkable events of historical happenstance, Charles II married the Portuguese Infanta Catharina in 1662. As part of the deal, Alfonso ceded control of Bombay, which became Charles's personal demesne, much to the dismay of the Viceroy of Goa, Antonio de Castro, who declared that the treaty would threaten the Portuguese presence in the region, not least by forcing vital legal issues over ownership onto the agenda. While the terms of the treaty were facilitated by shared legal traditions between the English and Portuguese, the practical realities facing Portuguese landowners who risked losing their estates were much less readily resolved, particularly since many were prepared to organise armed resistance.

Charles regarded Bombay as an expensive liability. Quite apart from the turmoil over landownership, there seemed little prospect of it becoming a major trading centre. He offered to sell the island back to the Portuguese crown, but the asking price was exorbitant. Instead, following lobbying, the Company stepped in to take control. And so it was that in 1668, under the terms of a royal charter, all rights, territories and appurtenances were transferred to the Company in return for an annuity of ten pounds. In language that revealed the extent to which the charter was conceived within English codes of common law dating back to the medieval period, Bombay would remain holden to Charles and his successors ‘as the Manor of East Greenwich, in free and common socage, and not in capite, not by knight’s service’ (John Marriott, Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, p. 158). In effect, this form of tenure exempted the Company from traditional obligations associated with landholding, including labour and military service.
Two views of the English fort at Bombay, published by Philip Baldaeus in 1672. The Company took control of Bombay in 1668, amid disputes over land held under Portuguese rule. Source: Philip Baldaeus/Wikimedia Commons.

The Company’s ambitions for Bombay were realised only gradually. Before fortification was completed early in the eighteenth century, the island faced serious problems. The expense of the fort itself, threats from external forces that resulted in its seizure in 1690, land reclamation and even a mutiny that resulted in the capture of the administration for a year all delayed the mission to develop the site as a major trading centre. Against this background emerged a renewed determination to exploit a long-held interest in Bengal. Following a disastrous attempt to capture Chittagong, the chief agent in the region, Job Charnock, sailed up the Ganges in 1690, looking for a suitable permanent site. He chose three small trading villages. At first glance, this pestilential settlement with few trading links was an unlikely option, but situated on the banks of the Ganges, with impenetrable jungle behind it, the site was defensible. Three years later, Charnock died, and so the reputation of this semi-mythical figure as the founder of Calcutta is somewhat misplaced, except that, in retrospect, his initial choice of the site was inspired.

Thus it was that Charles Eyre took over the administration and applied himself to the task of increasing revenue by acquiring land in the immediate vicinity. The three villages soon to become Calcutta were held by a Hindu family as a jaghir, originally granted by Jahangir in recognition of its help in defeating a local maharaja seeking independence. Under Mughal authority, rights to the land, although complicated, would not normally have been transferable to the Company. But events propelled a different course. 
Job Charnock’s tomb and epitaph in Kolkata. Charnock chose the site of the Company’s future Calcutta settlement. Source: Rangan Datta Wiki/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

In 1697, a revolt led by Subha Singh captured Bengal to the west of the Hugli River. The local nawab sought the help of British ships to defeat the rebels, which was agreed to on condition that full tenurial rights over Calcutta be conceded to the Company. These demands were denied; instead, inferior raiyat rights were offered and subsequently accepted, most likely because they included a provision to fortify the new factory. At this point, and with new confidence, Eyre sought to extend his territorial authority. Fully aware that zamindari rights would be resisted by local zamindars, he approached Prince Azim, the Viceroy of Bengal, who acceded to his wishes. Over the ensuing period, Fort William was completed; as in Madras, its protection attracted the settlement of artisans and labourers and attendant increases in revenue, while ever more land came under the control of the Company as zamindar. By 1717, following a concerted campaign of bribery and extortion, the Company received a farman bestowing the right to trade freely in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and to build a factory on any site of its choosing.

In a process more complicated than I have been able to convey in this short account, the East India Company established during the seventeenth century the necessary but not sufficient conditions for the acquisition of large swathes of India. Given the ignorance among factors of even the rudimentary features of English common law governing land, negotiations were likely pursued through corrupt and coercive means, particularly when advantageous opportunities opened up. The language of common law occasionally appeared in the drafting of agreements, but it was little more than window dressing to convey a spurious authority by lending legal legitimacy to arrangements whose practical foundations lay elsewhere.
 
A coloured engraving of Fort William in Bengal, belonging to the English East India Company. Printed for John Bowles, it is a reissue of the 1754 original by Jan van Ryne. Image: British Library

The Company’s territorial control was confined to small areas around what became the three great presidencies of Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, but the legal, ideological and economic foundations had been laid for the extraordinary land grab of the following centuries. In this respect, land was a vital aspect of Company endeavour. Without land, there was no protection or reliable source of revenue, and ultimately no empire. And yet land also exposed deep fault lines between commerce and conquest, London directors and factors, the Company and rival powers, and between policy and practice. These tensions were not incidental to the Company’s expansion. They were integral to it.

I have been conscious of the multidimensionality of land. If I have tended to focus on the legal and economic dimensions, it is because I lack the detailed knowledge of indigenous traditions of landownership and administration necessary for a detailed investigation of such aspects as identity, belonging and memory. I await with interest to see whether others better versed in indigenous land cultures rise to this challenge.

Professor John Marriott is a visiting fellow at Kellogg College, University of Oxford, and the author of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India (Cambridge University Press, 2025).

Since 1534, when Sultan Bahadur signed a treaty conferring rights on the Portuguese, the small island and port had languished through neglect and were generally considered to have few prospects. The beleaguered Company at Surat, however, looked to Bombay as a means of opening up trade along the west coast, but the Portuguese resisted any such move. Then, in one of those remarkable events of historical happenstance, Charles II married the Portuguese Infanta Catharina in 1662. As part of the deal, Alfonso ceded control of Bombay, which became Charles's personal demesne, much to the dismay of the Viceroy of Goa, Antonio de Castro, who declared that the treaty would threaten the Portuguese presence in the region, not least by forcing vital legal issues over ownership onto the agenda. While the terms of the treaty were facilitated by shared legal traditions between the English and Portuguese, the practical realities facing Portuguese landowners who risked losing their estates were much less readily resolved, particularly since many were prepared to organise armed resistance.

Charles regarded Bombay as an expensive liability. Quite apart from the turmoil over landownership, there seemed little prospect of it becoming a major trading centre. He offered to sell the island back to the Portuguese crown, but the asking price was exorbitant. Instead, following lobbying, the Company stepped in to take control. And so it was that in 1668, under the terms of a royal charter, all rights, territories and appurtenances were transferred to the Company in return for an annuity of ten pounds. In language that revealed the extent to which the charter was conceived within English codes of common law dating back to the medieval period, Bombay would remain holden to Charles and his successors ‘as the Manor of East Greenwich, in free and common socage, and not in capite, not by knight’s service’ (John Marriott, Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, p. 158). In effect, this form of tenure exempted the Company from traditional obligations associated with landholding, including labour and military service.

The Company’s ambitions for Bombay were realised only gradually. Before fortification was completed early in the eighteenth century, the island faced serious problems. The expense of the fort itself, threats from external forces that resulted in its seizure in 1690, land reclamation and even a mutiny that resulted in the capture of the administration for a year all delayed the mission to develop the site as a major trading centre. Against this background emerged a renewed determination to exploit a long-held interest in Bengal. Following a disastrous attempt to capture Chittagong, the chief agent in the region, Job Charnock, sailed up the Ganges in 1690, looking for a suitable permanent site. He chose three small trading villages. At first glance, this pestilential settlement with few trading links was an unlikely option, but situated on the banks of the Ganges, with impenetrable jungle behind it, the site was defensible. Three years later, Charnock died, and so the reputation of this semi-mythical figure as the founder of Calcutta is somewhat misplaced, except that, in retrospect, his initial choice of the site was inspired.

Thus it was that Charles Eyre took over the administration and applied himself to the task of increasing revenue by acquiring land in the immediate vicinity. The three villages soon to become Calcutta were held by a Hindu family as a jaghir, originally granted by Jahangir in recognition of its help in defeating a local maharaja seeking independence. Under Mughal authority, rights to the land, although complicated, would not normally have been transferable to the Company. But events propelled a different course.

In 1697, a revolt led by Subha Singh captured Bengal to the west of the Hugli River. The local nawab sought the help of British ships to defeat the rebels, which was agreed to on condition that full tenurial rights over Calcutta be conceded to the Company. These demands were denied; instead, inferior raiyat rights were offered and subsequently accepted, most likely because they included a provision to fortify the new factory. At this point, and with new confidence, Eyre sought to extend his territorial authority. Fully aware that zamindari rights would be resisted by local zamindars, he approached Prince Azim, the Viceroy of Bengal, who acceded to his wishes. Over the ensuing period, Fort William was completed; as in Madras, its protection attracted the settlement of artisans and labourers and attendant increases in revenue, while ever more land came under the control of the Company as zamindar. By 1717, following a concerted campaign of bribery and extortion, the Company received a farman bestowing the right to trade freely in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and to build a factory on any site of its choosing.

In a process more complicated than I have been able to convey in this short account, the East India Company established during the seventeenth century the necessary but not sufficient conditions for the acquisition of large swathes of India. Given the ignorance among factors of even the rudimentary features of English common law governing land, negotiations were likely pursued through corrupt and coercive means, particularly when advantageous opportunities opened up. The language of common law occasionally appeared in the drafting of agreements, but it was little more than window dressing to convey a spurious authority by lending legal legitimacy to arrangements whose practical foundations lay elsewhere.
 
A coloured engraving of Fort William in Bengal, belonging to the English East India Company. Printed for John Bowles, it is a reissue of the 1754 original by Jan van Ryne. Image: British Library

The Company’s territorial control was confined to small areas around what became the three great presidencies of Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, but the legal, ideological and economic foundations had been laid for the extraordinary land grab of the following centuries. In this respect, land was a vital aspect of Company endeavour. Without land, there was no protection or reliable source of revenue, and ultimately no empire. And yet land also exposed deep fault lines between commerce and conquest, London directors and factors, the Company and rival powers, and between policy and practice. These tensions were not incidental to the Company’s expansion. They were integral to it.

I have been conscious of the multidimensionality of land. If I have tended to focus on the legal and economic dimensions, it is because I lack the detailed knowledge of indigenous traditions of landownership and administration necessary for a detailed investigation of such aspects as identity, belonging and memory. I await with interest to see whether others better versed in indigenous land cultures rise to this challenge.

item.title: The Daily Star – Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq: Revisiting a complex legacy
item.description: One of the most influential political figures in the history of Bengal, Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq left an enduring legacy through his advocacy for peasant rights, his challenge to entrenched political and economic power, and his role in shaping the politics of colonial and postcolonial Bengal. Through a collection of essays and historical analyses, The Daily Star's Slow Reads revisits his life, political struggles, ideas and legacy, exploring how his vision and actions shaped Bengal's past and continue to resonate in Bangladesh today.

item.title: The Daily Star – Britain's love affair with curry and its colonial past
item.description:
In 2019, American academic Tim Nichols’ post on Twitter (now X), ‘Indian food is terrible and we pretend it isn’t’, sparked outrage across social media, raising concerns about racism, prejudice and the alienation of immigrants. Amidst a flurry of opinions both for and against, Britons emerged as some of the staunchest defenders of Indian cuisine. While Indian dishes are often a weekly staple in British households, with the much-loved pilau rice, madras, kormas, rogan joshes, jalfrezis, tikka masalas, samosas and bhajis sold as ready meals in supermarkets, the observance of ‘National Curry Week’ is an annual affair. The British nation’s fascination with Indian food had begun to take root during the eighteenth century as it emerged as a burgeoning imperial power; an appreciation of ‘curry’ thus often requires an appraisal of its more complex and, in many cases, unsavoury histories.

Beginnings of a culinary romance

Food is an inextricable part of colonial encounters and was central to experiencing foreign cultures. As Lizzie Collingham has shown, Edward Terry, chaplain at the embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to the Mughal court of Jahangir, was mesmerised by the sight of rice dishes served at banquets. While such high-end culinary adventures were awe-inspiring, ordinary everyday experiences were not short of wonder. James Forbes, who first arrived in 1765 at less than sixteen years of age to work as an East India Company writer, was fascinated by foodstuffs in western India. He documented natural life in his surroundings through text and images, and was particularly attentive to vegetables, grains and fruits. Adorning his thirteen-volume manuscripts and monumental four-volume Oriental Memoirs, pictures of local produce captured not only the diversity of India’s nature and culture but also how the coloniser wished to view them.
 
A portrait of James Forbes, published as the frontispiece to the first volume of his Oriental Memoirs in 1813. His writings and illustrations documented aspects of Indian society, culture and natural history.

A particular item that attracted Forbes’ attention was the mango, which he was strongly in favour of importing to England. He had struggled to explain the taste of mangoes in letters to his friends and family but depicted the fruit in a familiar still-life format so that it could immediately appeal to a European audience as an exotic delight. Forbes was also intrigued by Indian cooking techniques, especially how spices were prepared, combined and stirred into delicious, curried concoctions. If curries might have tantalised Forbes’ taste buds, the delectable sweetness of mangoes would have soothed his constitution, as he was keen on several recipes involving mangoes, from preserves to chutneys and everything in between.

A spicy dalliance deepens

While the British and other Europeans have understood curry as quintessentially South Asian, the concept of curry itself is rather unfamiliar to Indians in the subcontinent. Some writings have pointed to the Tamil word ‘kari’ or the Portuguese adaptation ‘caril’, but stews, relishes and gravies eaten all over South Asia are far too varied to be generalised as such. When I spotted curry powder on supermarket shelves for the first time in my life after arriving in continental Europe as a university student, I was a bit surprised – and disappointed when I checked the list of ingredients on the label. Finding good-quality garam masala was no easy feat either; but it was less of an issue, as every family has its own unique blend of spices that are sourced from specialist suppliers and then carefully threshed, roasted, powdered and stored in sealed containers.
 
James Forbes’ illustration of mangoes from Oriental Memoirs (1813), reflecting his interest in India’s natural history and the botanical observations recorded during his travels.

My own culinary curiosity, coupled with the need to introduce and discuss Indian food with European coursemates and colleagues, made me explore curry powder further and led me back again to the eighteenth century. Curry powder emerged in this era, as Indian food increasingly interested Britons. Linda Colley, in her book Captives: Britain, Empire, and the World, 1600–1850, mentions Sarah Shade, who, having confronted war and conflict in India, catered to the oriental tastes of British officials returning home by serving vegetable curries. The frontispiece of Hannah Glasse’s cookbook, featuring the recipe ‘To make a Currey the Indian Way’, shows a scullery maid in the background who is about to prepare poultry, perhaps to cook a chicken curry. Both meat and vegetarian options were already on the menu. In 1810, Sake Dean Mahomed went on to establish Britain’s first curry house in Portman Square, London.

A complicated relationship

Beneath the British obsession with curries, however, lie narratives that mostly escape our attention. While elaborate balls, feasts and parties were indispensable to the social lives of colonial officials, restrictions had come to be imposed on Indian royalty and nobility. For example, the Nawab of Murshidabad, Mubarak ud-Daulah, faced stark criticism from Governor-General Warren Hastings for his spending on local religious festivities; in fact, these acts of patronage had been integral to rulers’ obligations to their subjects for ages. 
 
Nawab Mubarak ud-Daulah receives the British Resident, Sir John Hadley D’Oyly, at his court in Murshidabad. The late eighteenth-century painting depicts a ruler whose spending on local religious festivities drew criticism from Governor-General Warren Hastings. Source: British Library/Wikimedia Commons

At the other end of the social scale, colonial extraction resulted in famines and outbreaks of diseases that destabilised Indian society and its economy. Farmers and cultivators were disparaged as either being too lazy, given the fertility of the soil, or their never-ending toil was highlighted as the plight of living under despotic governments. 

However, as almost 150 years of Indian economic scholarship has shown, it was the overweening tax burden of the Raj that reduced investment and productivity on the land. In such a scenario, it is hardly surprising that the introduction of new high-calorie crops such as potatoes was often championed as a boon of British governance. A later, exiled Nawab of Lucknow, Wajid Ali Shah, was reputed to have incorporated potatoes into his household’s biryani both as a response to fiscal pressure and as a culinary innovation. The variation remains a Bengali delicacy.

By the late 1780s, as the British had already begun to distance themselves from Indian life and culture, their attitude towards Indian cuisine also began to change. The diplomatic exchange of fruits, practised widely amongst Indian rulers, lost its sentimental value as the colonial state cultivated an image of being free from corruption. Food gifts also became a source of colonial anxiety, as Lord Valentia, during his travels across northern India, was baffled by the opulence of the delicacies presented to him by local dignitaries and often gave them away to his native servants. 
 
Sake Dean Mahomed (1759–1851), born in Patna, Bihar, was an Indian traveller, writer and entrepreneur who helped introduce Indian cuisine and culture to Britain.

The second half of the nineteenth century saw the British gradually shifting towards European menus at banquets in India, especially with French haute cuisine gaining pride of place. Not coincidentally, these social circles spent their summers in hill stations very close to tea plantations.

Curries, nevertheless, remained popular back in Britain. As Queen Victoria assumed the title of Empress of India in 1876, her interest in Indian life found expression in the magnificent Durbar Room at Osborne House. She was also fond of curry. Curries soon entered middle-class households and became part of the British imagination, so much so that, for instance, they were among Sherlock Holmes's favourite dishes. In The Adventure of Silver Blaze, the reference to curry helped the detective crack a mysterious case of intoxication. Holmes also feasted on a plate of curried fowl prepared by the housekeeper in the happy ending to The Adventure of the Naval Treaty. 
The first recipe for curry published in Britain appeared in Hannah Glasse’s The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy in 1747. Shown here are the book’s frontispiece and the original recipe. Source: Wikimedia Commons

Curry's widespread popularity, however, came at a cost. While the adaptation of individual recipes to local palates is inevitable, the twentieth-century practice of branding curries in eateries as mild, medium and hot has obscured much of their culinary diversity. Besides their socio-cultural complexities, Indian food takes a great deal of thought, labour and time to prepare. Reducing curries to 'sauces' and naming them after regions might seem efficient, but is ultimately a disservice to the ethos of South Asian communities that have treasured diverse culinary knowledge, methods and techniques across multiple lands and generations.

Healthy boundaries beyond curry

In line with developments in other disciplines, curry enthusiasts now talk about decolonising the cuisine. Amidst such deliberations, let's try to go beyond the 'curry' label and ask ourselves: are there any decent South Asian dishes other than curries? There are so many of them that one would never even need to fabricate something like Jamdani Haansh ('duck in sari'), favoured by Nessa in the British sitcom Gavin and Stacey! With the Indian food scene rapidly changing in the West, one might be pleasantly surprised by the diversity of dishes available beyond the familiar curry.
 
The cover of Linda Colley’s Captives: Britain, Empire and the World 1600–1850, published by Pimlico in 2003.

Transcending the limits of curry would also help us find inspiration in South Asian cultures' emphasis on cooking with diverse plant-based ingredients. This is important partly because the link between regular consumption of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of chronic diseases has now been well established. Gut health experts have come to suggest increasing the variety of plants we eat on a weekly basis, advocating the inclusion of herbs and spices in our regular diets. The adaptation of diverse diets thus requires us to acknowledge and engage more meaningfully with the cultural diversity around us.

Thinking about the history of 'curry' in this way must go beyond textual documentation stripped of its social and colonial contexts, or the mere recreation of past recipes. Instead, it would be essential to shed light on the cultural aesthetics of the various ingredients and their emotional and sensory dimensions. Learning about Indian cuisine on its own terms would be a productive way to enrich discussions on multiculturalism, food resilience, sustainability, nutrition and more inclusive futures.

Dr Apurba Chatterjee is a Visiting Research Fellow in the Department of History at the University of Reading, UK.
